title: Breaking the habit. A commentary on ‘Fossil flowers of Ayenia (Malvaceae) preserved in amber: evidence for lianas in Miocene rainforest of Southeast China’
content: It is not uncommon for palaeobotanists to use the systematic placement of a fossil flower, leaf or fruit to infer attributes about the whole plant, including the broad growth habit – for example, whether an extinct taxon was probably herbaceous or woody – but what evidence is necessary to suggest a more nuanced habit? In this issue of the Annals of Botany, Wu et al. (2026) describe two fossil flowers, Ayenia zhangpuensis and Ayenia sp., both of which are trapped in Miocene (∼14.7 Mya, Zheng et al., 2019) amber from Southeast China and were described by Wu et al. (2026) as ‘exquisitely preserved’. The preservation in amber has three-dimensionally captured the morphological characters of the flower in a life-like orientation, providing an excellent opportunity to study the fossils in meticulous detail. This has resulted in a well-developed analysis of the fossil material and comparison to extant flowers of the Malvaceae and particularly to the genus Ayenia section Vahihara. Based on the taxonomic placement of these new fossil flowers the authors suggest that they provide evidence for the presence of lianas in the rainforest of the Zhangpu palaeobiota. This conclusion prompts consideration of the type and extent of evidence necessary to infer a particular habit, like the liana habit, and to extrapolate from that inference to the vegetation structure and ecology of the surrounding palaeoecosystem.
